notes: Landmark BIT arbitration non-justiciability ruling; Aikens J held section 67 challenge to UNCITRAL award was justiciable.

enrichment.short_title: Ecuador v Occidental: non-justiciability and BIT arbitration awards in London
key_facts: Occidental, a US oil investor, obtained a UNCITRAL arbitration award in London against Ecuador under the US-Ecuador Bilateral Investment Treaty over denied VAT refunds on oil exports.
The tribunal awarded Occidental over US$75 million; Ecuador challenged the award under section 67 on jurisdictional grounds.
Occidental contended the English court could not interpret the unincorporated BIT and must dismiss Ecuador's challenge as non-justiciable.
London was the seat of the arbitration and Part I of the 1996 Act applied.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Preliminary application to strike out Ecuador's section 67 challenge to a BIT arbitration award on non-justiciability grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Occidental's application dismissed; the court may entertain Ecuador's section 67 challenge despite the need to interpret an unincorporated treaty.
enrichment.ratio: The doctrine of non-justiciability does not prevent an English court from determining a section 67 challenge to an arbitral award where rights with origins in international law are exercised through a London-seated arbitration subject to municipal procedural law; section 67 provides the domestic law foothold to construe the BIT as necessary.
legal_issues: Whether rights under a BIT are public international law or private municipal law rights
Whether municipal courts may interpret unincorporated treaties between foreign states
Whether non-justiciability bars a section 67 jurisdictional challenge to a BIT award
Whether enforcement under section 101 would likewise require treaty interpretation

notes: Anti-war protest harassment injunction; Gross J granted limited interim relief under the 1997 Act balancing Articles 10 and 11.

enrichment.short_title: EDO v Smash EDO: harassment injunction against Brighton defence-industry protesters

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: EDO MBM, a Brighton defence contractor, and its managing director sought interim injunctions against anti-Iraq war protesters under the Protection from Harassment Act 1997.
Protests included road obstruction, roof trespass, criminal damage, home leafleting and intimidation of employees.
Individual defendants had convictions for obstruction or aggravated trespass; Smash EDO was struck out as an unincorporated association without representatives.
Defendants argued the Act should not restrict legitimate political protest protected by Articles 10 and 11 ECHR.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interim injunction and strike-out applications in civil harassment proceedings after related criminal convictions.
enrichment.outcome: Interim injunction granted in trimmed terms against most individual defendants; relief refused against acquitted defendants; Smash EDO and BOOB struck out.
enrichment.ratio: The Protection from Harassment Act may restrain apprehended harassment in protest contexts where conduct crosses into targeting employees and directors, but restrictions must satisfy the enhanced Cyanamid/Cream Holdings test and be proportionate to Articles 10 and 11 rights.
legal_issues: Whether companies may claim under the Protection from Harassment Act 1997
Whether unincorporated associations may be sued without representative defendants
The test for interim injunctions engaging Article 10 where breach carries criminal penalties
Whether apprehended harassment requires a prior course of conduct

notes: Licensing appeal by case stated; Mitting J upheld fit-and-proper finding despite licensee dishonesty to police.

enrichment.short_title: Leicestershire Police v Tatam: fit-and-proper test for justices' on-licence
key_facts: Shirley Tatam applied for a justices' on-licence for the Ashby Woulds public house under a deemed interim authority.
Licensing Committee found she had been aggressive to council officers in May 2004 and lied to police, but preferred officers' evidence on the incident.
Despite discredit, the committee found she was fit and proper because the premises had been well run for nearly five months.
Leicestershire Police appealed by case stated contending the decision was perverse.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from a licensing committee grant of a justices' on-licence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; costs ordered against the police because the appeal had no prospect of success.
enrichment.ratio: The fit-and-proper person test under section 3(1) of the Licensing Act 1964 asks whether the applicant can be relied on to run licensed premises competently and lawfully; a committee may grant a licence despite dishonesty if overall conduct demonstrates reliable management.
legal_issues: The correct test for a fit and proper licensee under section 3(1)
Whether dishonesty to police necessarily precludes a fit-and-proper finding
Whether the committee's decision was perverse
Costs on licensing appeals raising genuine police concerns

notes: Adverse possession appeal; Court of Appeal held occupation was with implied permission under Limitation Act 1980 Sch 1 para 8(4).

enrichment.short_title: Batsford Estates v Taylor: implied permission and adverse possession of farm property
key_facts: The Taylor family occupied the Old Farmhouse and related land at Aston Magna under a series of mistaken tenancy agreements after surrendering a larger farm tenancy in 1970.
A 1985 notice to quit was served but the estate allowed the Taylors to remain; only one peppercorn rent payment was accepted.
Algy Taylor's son claimed title by twelve years' adverse possession from October 1985; the recorder ordered possession for Batsford Estates.
The dispute covered the farmhouse, farmyard and adjoining orchard and paddock.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from county court possession proceedings on adverse possession and implied permission.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Algy Taylor's occupation was by implied permission of the estate and could not amount to adverse possession.
enrichment.ratio: Under paragraph 8(4) of schedule 1 to the Limitation Act 1980 a finding of implied permission is justified where demonstrable circumstances show the landowner accepted the status quo and a reasonable person would appreciate occupation was permitted, applying Etherton J's two-part test.
legal_issues: Whether occupation after a defective notice to quit was adverse possession
The test for implied permission under schedule 1 paragraph 8(4)
Whether tenant encroachment on adjoining landlord land is presumed part of the demise
Effect of mistaken life-tenancy agreements on animus possidendi

notes: SEN statutory assessment appeal; Sullivan J dismissed challenge to tribunal's rejection of expert evidence.

enrichment.short_title: R (A) v Lambeth: refusal of statutory special educational needs assessment
key_facts: A, an eight-year-old with speech, language and behavioural difficulties, attended a mainstream primary school in Lambeth.
His father, the sole carer after family breakdown, requested a statutory assessment under section 329; the LEA refused.
The SEN tribunal accepted school provision including weekly speech therapy but disagreed with privately commissioned expert reports recommending a full assessment.
Expert reports from a speech therapist and educational psychologist were not contradicted but were rejected on professional judgment grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 11 appeal from a special educational needs tribunal dismissal of a section 329 assessment request.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the tribunal adequately explained its limited disagreement with the experts and applied the Code of Practice test.
enrichment.ratio: A SEN tribunal may reject uncontradicted expert evidence if it states its disagreement and explains why existing school provision meets the section 324/Code paragraph 7.34 test; limited disputes over session length or delivery method need not be elaborately reasoned.
legal_issues: Whether the tribunal gave adequate reasons for rejecting expert reports
The test for ordering a statutory assessment under section 324 and the SEN Code
Whether SAT progress alone could justify refusing assessment
The extent of tribunal expertise when evaluating educational provision

notes: JDS press-notice trial; Laddie J held publication power existed and public interest outweame confidentiality.

enrichment.short_title: Deloitte v JDS: breach of confidence over accountancy disciplinary press notice
key_facts: The Joint Disciplinary Scheme investigated Deloitte's audit work for Capital Corporation and partner Stephen Ives, who was later excluded for fraud.
Executive Counsel Christopher Dickson proposed a press notice announcing complaints against Deloitte and chairman Martin Scicluna before tribunal hearing.
Deloitte obtained without-notice injunctions restraining publication, arguing the JDS lacked power and the notice breached Regulation 52 confidentiality.
The application was treated as the trial of the action.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of action for permanent injunction and declaration restraining JDS press notice prior to disciplinary tribunal.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the Executive Committee had power to issue the press notice and publication was justified in the public interest despite limited confidential content.
enrichment.ratio: The JDS Executive Committee may publish interim press notices under paragraph 5d(xii) to maintain public confidence in accountancy regulation; Regulation 52 confidentiality does not prevent publication where balancing Article 10 interests favours accurate public disclosure of complaint summaries.
legal_issues: Whether the JDS Executive Committee had power to issue a pre-tribunal press notice
Whether investigation information was confidential under Regulation 52
Balancing confidentiality against freedom of expression in professional discipline
Whether redacted notices would cause greater reputational harm than full summaries

notes: Norwich Pharmacal application refused; Lightman J held Mitsui should seek pre-action disclosure from EnCana Corp instead.

enrichment.short_title: Mitsui v Nexen: Norwich Pharmacal relief and Buzzard Field sale protocol
key_facts: Mitsui negotiated to buy EnCana's UK subsidiary holding a major interest in the Buzzard oil field but EnCana sold to Nexen for $2.1 billion in October 2004.
Mitsui alleged an oral Protocol Agreement under which EnCana would not solicit third-party offers and would notify bona fide competing bids.
Mitsui sought Norwich Pharmacal disclosure from Nexen's UK subsidiary about how Nexen's bid arose to support a breach-of-contract claim against EnCana Corp.
EnCana denied the Protocol and said post-approach negotiation was permitted once an unsolicited offer was received.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for Norwich Pharmacal disclosure and affidavit evidence against a non-party target company.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; pre-action disclosure from EnCana Corp was the appropriate and available remedy and the defendant was not mixed up in solicitation.
enrichment.ratio: Norwich Pharmacal relief against an innocent third party is a remedy of last resort requiring necessity where no other practicable source exists; CPR 31.16 pre-action disclosure from the likely defendant displaces the jurisdiction, and the First Limb of a non-solicitation pact restricts solicitation not subsequent negotiation of unsolicited offers.
legal_issues: Whether Norwich Pharmacal disclosure was necessary against a non-party target company
Availability of CPR 31.16 pre-action disclosure against EnCana Corp
Construction of a non-solicitation limb in an oral protocol agreement
Whether the defendant was mixed up in alleged breach of the protocol

notes: Police injury pension appeal; Court of Appeal held medical referee decides disablement at date of decision not SMP certificate.

enrichment.short_title: McGinley v Schilling: medical referee's date for police injury pension appeals
key_facts: Two retired Metropolitan Police officers appealed certificates of selected medical practitioners fixing degrees of disablement at 35% and 45%.
Medical referees disagreed on whether they should review disablement as at the SMP's date or at the appeal hearing date.
McCombe J held Regulation H2 required a contemporary determination; the Commissioner appealed.
Schedule H permits further interviews and fresh evidence before the medical referee.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Joined appeals from Administrative Court judicial review upholding medical referee decisions on pension disablement appeals.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; a medical referee under Regulation H2 determines disablement as at the date of the referee's decision on up-to-date evidence.
enrichment.ratio: Regulation H2 appeals are rehearings, not mere reviews; Regulation A12(1) and A20 require disablement to be assessed when the question arises for decision, which for appeals is the medical referee's determination date, and all Regulation H1(2) questions should be answered consistently as at that date.
legal_issues: Whether a medical referee is confined to reviewing the SMP certificate at its date
Application of Regulation A12(1) to medical referee decisions
Relationship between Regulation H2 appeals and Regulation K2 periodic reviews
Whether degree-of-disablement questions under H1(2)(d) differ from other H1 questions

notes: Insurance broker summary judgment refused; Gloster J found limitation and causation disputes arguable on misrepresentation fax.

enrichment.short_title: Gaughan v McDonagh: hotel fire insurance broker negligence and policy avoidance
key_facts: Broker Tony McDonagh placed fire insurance for the Newbury Hotel in Margate but the property was omitted from the initial policy schedule.
On 11 November 1998 the broker faxed insurers describing tenants as elderly DSS-funded occupants rather than homeless people of all ages.
A fire on 21 November 1998 caused about £400,000 damage; Norwich Union avoided the policy ab initio for misrepresentation.
The claimant sued the broker for failing accurately to communicate material risk information.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Defendant's CPR Part 24 summary judgment and Part 3.4 strike-out application in broker negligence claim.
enrichment.outcome: Both applications dismissed; limitation and causation issues required trial and the 11 November fax breach was arguably not time-barred.
enrichment.ratio: Where the pleaded broker breach is a continuing misdescription on a specific later date rather than defective placement at inception, limitation may run from that breach; summary judgment fails where disputes exist over whether insurers would have avoided the policy in any event for non-disclosure.
legal_issues: When a broker negligence cause of action accrues for limitation purposes
Whether misdescribing occupancy on 11 November 1998 was a separate continuing duty breach
Causation where insurers might have avoided for other non-disclosure grounds
Availability of lost-opportunity damages if the risk would have been declined

notes: Defamation summary procedure; Eady J awarded maximum statutory damages and falsity declaration against defaulting US author.

enrichment.short_title: Bin Mahfouz v Ehrenfeld: terrorism funding libel and summary disposal
key_facts: Dr Rachel Ehrenfeld's book Funding Evil alleged Saudi businessman Khalid Bin Mahfouz and his sons financed Al Qaeda through NCB and charities.
The book was sold in England via online retailers and chapter one appeared on ABCnews.com; defendants did not defend after default judgment.
Claimants denied terrorism links and addressed prior purported justification points including BCCI, Muwafaq and alleged 1999 NCB audit.
Ehrenfeld later sued KBM in New York claiming English libel law chilled investigation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Summary disposal application under sections 8-10 Defamation Act 1996 after default judgment and injunction.
enrichment.outcome: Maximum summary damages of £10,000 each, declaration of falsity, costs on account £30,000, and order to publish correction and apology.
enrichment.ratio: Where defendants have no real prospect of defending serious terrorism-funding allegations and have not pleaded justification despite opportunity, sections 8-10 summary procedure appropriately vindicates reputation with a declaration of falsity based on explicit claimant evidence rather than presumption alone.
legal_issues: Whether defendants had a real prospect of successfully defending the libel claim
Appropriate use of summary disposal after default judgment against foreign defendants
Meaning of allegations that claimants funded Al Qaeda and related terrorist organisations
Assessment of damages under the statutory summary procedure cap
